Everyday life · 15 November 2026

Shorter days: light, sleep and mood in autumn

With fewer hours of daylight, many people feel sleepier and less energetic. What is normal and when to seek advice.

In November the sun rises late and sets early. Many people find it harder to get up, feel sleepier in the afternoon or are less inclined to go out. It is not just an impression.

Light sets the clock

Our body clock synchronises mainly with morning light. When less light reaches us, or it arrives later, sleep–wake rhythms tend to drift and melatonin secretion lasts longer. Spending the day indoors, where light is far dimmer than outside even on a cloudy day, adds to the effect.

When it is something more

In 1984 Norman Rosenthal and his team described people who had a depressive episode every autumn or winter that lifted in spring. Diagnostic manuals now include it as depression with a seasonal pattern. It is more common at high latitudes and is not the same as an ordinary autumn slump: it involves persistent sadness, loss of interest and real difficulty in daily life.

What tends to help

  • Going outside in the morning, even briefly.
  • Keeping regular sleep times, weekends included.
  • Staying physically active and keeping in touch with other people.

Bright light therapy has been studied for seasonal depression with favourable results, but it should be prescribed and supervised by a professional. If low mood lasts more than two weeks or gets in the way of your life, talk to your family doctor.

References

  1. Rosenthal, N. E. et al. (1984). Seasonal affective disorder. Archives of General Psychiatry, 41(1), 72–80.
  2. Pjrek, E. et al. (2020). The efficacy of light therapy in the treatment of seasonal affective disorder: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics, 89(1), 17–24.
